bp: A researcher writing a paper faces a practical navigation problem. The useful prior work is scattered across a fast-growing web of academic publications, and the author often needs different kinds of references at different moments: a broad list of related papers for a topic, and a precise citation for one sentence or paragraph. This paper builds CiteRAG to test whether large language models can help with that job by first finding candidate papers and then suggesting citations. The important object is not just a document collection; it is a draft in motion, where each citation should connect a local claim to earlier work. The benchmark turns citation prediction into two tasks: coarse list-specific prediction and fine position-specific prediction. It also supplies a large three-level corpus of 554,000 papers and datasets with 7,267 and 8,541 task instances, so citation help can be evaluated as both search and generation rather than as a one-off text answer.
wh: Citation prediction is hard because relevance changes with context. A prior paper may be useful because it introduced a problem, supplied a method, reported a dataset, gave a baseline, or offered a result that the current sentence is comparing against. The same candidate reference can be right in one part of a manuscript and wrong in another. The scale makes the problem worse: with hundreds of thousands of papers in the corpus, a system cannot read and deeply compare every possible reference whenever an author needs help. The abstract also separates two levels of difficulty. In list-specific prediction, the system must gather a sensible set of papers for a broader writing need. In position-specific prediction, it must decide what belongs at a particular citation location. Those are not identical decisions. A broad related-work list can tolerate several neighboring papers; a citation after a precise claim needs sharper evidence and better local fit.
naive: A smart beginner would search the paper draft with keywords, collect the top matching papers, and ask a language model to choose from them. That works when the draft and the prior work use the same words, and when the citation need is broad. It fails when two fields use different vocabulary for the same idea, when a paper should be cited for a small technical role rather than its title words, or when many candidates share common phrases. Another simple plan is to copy citations from similar papers. That can recover familiar references, but it may repeat old habits, miss newer work, and ignore the exact sentence where the citation is needed. The paper's benchmark exists because citation quality depends on both finding the right candidates and placing them in the right writing context.
ap: The core idea is to treat citation suggestion as a retrieve-then-write problem. First, a retrieval system searches a large academic corpus at multiple levels, so it can gather evidence that matches both broad paper-level needs and finer local citation positions. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, means the language model is not asked to answer from memory alone; it is given retrieved papers as outside evidence before producing suggestions. CiteRAG also uses specialized retrievers and generators, so the component that searches and the component that writes can be tuned for citation prediction rather than treated as a generic question-answering pipeline. The abstract says the retrieval model is fine-tuned with contrastive learning: examples of real citation relationships teach the system which paper pairs should be pulled closer for comparison and which should be kept apart. The final benchmark evaluates both stages, because a fluent generator cannot repair a missing candidate, and a good candidate list still needs context-aware selection.
mech: The mechanism begins with a citation prediction instance from an academic writing setting. For the coarse task, the input represents a broader list-specific need: which references belong with this paper or section-level context. For the fine task, the input represents a position-specific need: which reference fits a particular place in the manuscript. The system then searches a three-level corpus containing 554,000 papers across major subfields. Multi-level retrieval means the search does not rely on one flat pass over the whole collection; it can use broader and narrower views of the literature so candidates are gathered at the right grain. Each candidate paper and each query context must be turned into a comparable description. The specialized retriever scores candidates by how well their learned descriptions match the citation context. Fine-tuning with contrastive learning adjusts those descriptions using real citation links: cited or otherwise related examples are treated as matches, while unsuitable examples are treated as nonmatches. After retrieval, a specialized generation model receives the writing context together with the candidate papers. It produces citation predictions for the required task, such as a list of likely references or a suggestion for a specific citation position. The benchmark records whether both retrieval and generation succeed, using the 7,267 coarse instances and 8,541 fine instances to test the two levels separately.
math: The main mathematical ideas are similarity, ranking, learning from paired examples, and conditional generation. Similarity is the decision that two pieces of writing should be treated as near because they play related scholarly roles, even if their surface words differ. The retriever must compress a draft context and a paper into numeric descriptions, often called embeddings, meaning lists of numbers that make comparison cheap. That compression is useful because the corpus is large, but it can lose the reason a citation matters. Ranking then sorts thousands of possible references by score, asking which few deserve attention first. Contrastive learning is comparison-based training: the model sees pairs that should be close, such as a citation context and a paper actually cited there, and pairs that should be farther apart. It changes its comparison rule so real citation relationships score better than misleading neighbors. The generation stage adds a probability problem: given the local context and retrieved evidence, it estimates which citation output is most plausible. The tradeoff is reach versus faithfulness. Broad retrieval helps avoid missing papers, while fine position-specific scoring tries to avoid suggestions that are topically related but wrong for the sentence.
dots: This paper belongs to the repo's retrieval-augmented generation family because it makes outside documents control what a language model can sensibly suggest. Like other RAG work, it starts from the failure of memory-only answers: the model needs current, specific evidence from a collection before it can be trusted. It also connects directly to the similarity concept, since citation prediction depends on building a map where a draft passage and its useful prior papers land near one another for the right scholarly reason. It connects to ranking because the system must choose a small reference set from a 554,000-paper corpus; the practical decision is which candidates rise to the top. Compared with RAG papers about conflict, document quality, graph evidence, or efficient retrieval, CiteRAG's pressure is academic attribution. The recurring problem is still the same: search must shrink a huge evidence pile before generation, and the shrinkage is dangerous if it removes the paper that would justify the claim.
ww: The approach should work better than keyword search because real citations are repeated evidence about scholarly relatedness. If many past papers cite a work in contexts that resemble the current context, that pattern teaches more than shared words alone. Fine-tuning the retriever with contrastive examples turns citation links into training pressure: the system is rewarded for placing truly related citation contexts and papers closer together, and penalized for confusing nearby but uncited or less appropriate papers. Multi-level retrieval helps because citation decisions happen at more than one grain. A broad pass can find papers that belong to the general topic, while a finer pass can favor papers that support a particular local claim. The generator then has a narrower, evidence-rich set to reason over, so it is less dependent on vague model memory. The benchmark design is part of the benefit: by separating coarse list-specific and fine position-specific tasks, it can reveal whether a model is merely finding related literature or actually choosing citations where writers need them.
po: The payoff is a reproducible way to test and build citation assistants for academic writing. CiteRAG supplies two citation prediction tasks, thousands of task instances, a three-level corpus of 554,000 papers, specialized retrieval and generation components, and an open-source toolkit. That lets researchers compare closed-source APIs, open-source models, and fine-tuned generators on the same evidence-grounded problem. For authors, the hoped-for capability is more complete and better placed references: fewer missed prior works, less manual searching, and citation suggestions that account for both the paper's broad topic and the exact position where a reference is needed.
limits: The abstract supports the benchmark and system design, but it does not prove that suggested citations are correct for every field, writing style, or kind of scholarly contribution. The method assumes the corpus contains the relevant prior work and that citation links in the data are good enough training signals. Real citation behavior can be incomplete, biased toward famous papers, or shaped by venue habits rather than perfect relevance. The generated suggestions also depend on retrieval quality; if the right paper is not retrieved, the generator has little basis for naming it. The abstract mentions extensive experiments but does not give detailed error cases, human judgments, or evidence that authors would accept the suggestions in real drafting.
